item.title: UniSD: Towards a Unified Self-Distillation Framework for Large Language Models
item.description:
Abstract

Self-distillation offers a promising path for adapting large language models without stronger external teachers, but it remains hard to apply reliably in autoregressive LLMs. We propose UniSD, a unified framework that systematically studies self-distillation by integrating complementary mechanisms — multi-teacher agreement, EMA teacher stabilization, token-level contrastive learning, feature matching, and divergence clipping. Across six benchmarks and six models from three families, UniSD clarifies when and why self-distillation helps, and its integrated pipeline improves over the base model by +5.4 points and the strongest baseline by +2.8 points.

item.title: CultivAgents: Cultivating Relationship-Centered Multi-Agent Systems for Personalized Gardening
item.description:
Abstract

Gardening supports well-being, cultural continuity, and food autonomy, yet digital tools often give generic advice that overlooks gardeners’ skills, local ecologies, and cultural contexts. We introduce CultivAgents, a relationship-centered multi-agent system grounded in ethics of care that coordinates an Experience Agent, an Environmental Agent, and an Ethnobotanical Agent to deliver personalized, socio-culturally grounded support. A three-phase mixed-methods study with experts, HCI researchers, and community gardeners found that CultivAgents helped gardeners translate interest into situated action and increased their confidence, motivation, and trust in acting on AI advice.

item.title: Science Utopia? Closed-Loop LLM Simulation of Academic Research Ecosystems
item.description:
Science Utopia is a persistent, closed-loop LLM-agent simulation for studying how academic research ecosystems evolve. Research direction, collaboration, submission, peer review, resubmission, citation, funding, and researcher attrition feed back into one another across simulated years.

The framework supports controlled comparisons of institutional policies and research strategies. Its simulations examine how resubmission affects reviewer workload, how exploration shapes research impact and diversity, and how resource inequality emerges over time.

My role. Co-first author, with equal contribution.

item.title: PersonaCUABench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents Serving Diverse Personas
item.description:
PersonaCUABench evaluates computer-use agents through the people they serve. It holds tasks fixed while varying user personas, letting agents interact with requests that may omit requirements, add constraints, or call for approval before consequential actions.

The benchmark distinguishes task completion from meeting a user’s expressed needs, examining both agent performance and user satisfaction.

item.title: Do As I Do, Not As I Say: On-Policy Distillation Inherits the Teacher in Vision-Language Models
item.description:
This work compares on-policy distillation with filtered supervised fine-tuning in vision-language models. It examines how teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories affects both answer accuracy and the ability to complete a response.

The results show that on-policy supervision can transfer persistent teacher failure modes as well as knowledge, making teacher reliability on student-visited states central to successful distillation.

item.title: From Knowledge Access to Source Learning: Developing Source-Specific Competence
item.description:
SourceLearn studies how LLM agents can progressively learn from a persistent authoritative source. It builds a reusable source model that represents how knowledge is structured, interpreted, and applied.

Self-directed learning revisits incompletely understood material, while task-guided learning uses downstream experience to identify gaps. Updates remain grounded in the authoritative source.

item.title: TextReg: Mitigating Prompt Distributional Overfitting via Regularized Text-Space Optimization
item.description:
Abstract

LLMs are highly sensitive to their prompts, and iterative prompt-optimization methods often overfit: prompts grow longer, accumulate sample-specific rules, and generalize poorly. We study this as prompt distributional overfitting and introduce TextReg, a regularization framework that realizes a soft-penalty objective through regularized textual gradients — combining Dual-Evidence Gradient Purification, Semantic Edit Regularization, and Regularization-Guided Prompt Update. Across reasoning benchmarks, TextReg improves out-of-distribution generalization by up to +11.8% over TextGrad and +16.5% over REVOLVE.
